extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political theory, policymakers, and those interested in public administration
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for assessing the quality and organisation of public administration in parliamentary versus bureaucratic systems—covers ministerial turnover, parliamentary oversight, bureaucracy defects, and the proper roles of ministers and permanent officials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bringing in untried persons
rubrics_metrics.description: Sudden, wholesale changes of ministers bring in new and untried persons to preside over policy; they often have not been previously engaged with the department's subject and are not 'part and parcel' of its mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explained via example of Lord Cranborne suddenly made Indian Secretary: able men can 'get up' a subject but lack ingrained familiarity. Matching many offices at once is difficult (like a Chinese puzzle); vacancies rarely have twenty tried competent men ready. Antipatterns: appointing ministers with no subject experience simply because of party expediency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indifference of incumbent ministers
rubrics_metrics.description: If ministers know their tenure can be cut short by events beyond their control, they lack the strongest motives to learn their tasks thoroughly and can become indifferent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: New appointees may be eager, but many (especially older or 'battered' ministers) focus more on political vicissitudes than on office business. This disincentive reduces administrative care and long-term attention to departmental improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy continuity and loss of accumulated experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Rapid succession of chiefs disrupts continuity of policy; a continuity of mediocrity may be preferable to a patchwork of transient excellences because long experience produces a 'nicely balanced mind' that anticipates errors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: military procurement and technical progress suffer if each new head cannot learn from predecessors; analogy of new head boy failing to benefit from experience of previous head boy. Antipatterns: expecting quick succession of ministers to collectively produce cumulative expertise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parliamentary inquisitiveness and its effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Parliament, being a large and active assembly, will inquire into and meddle in many departmental matters; this curiosity creates pressure on departments to justify actions and can expose them to hostile selection of criticism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characterised as 'a big meeting of more or less idle people' with unlimited curiosity—ministers must answer detailed questions on many subjects. Consequences include selective attacks by opposition, press amplification, motions for inquiry, and public scandal; departments without effective spokesmen are vulnerable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for a Parliamentary head/party protector
rubrics_metrics.description: A Parliamentary head (a ministerial, party-connected defender) protects a department from parliamentary attacks and busybodies, marshals support, compiles counter-arguments, and secures votes to preserve consistent policy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Described as a 'protecting machine' that studies subjects, compiles statistics, and organizes supporters (example: Secretary of the Treasury arranging bench support). The Poor Law administration is cited: when it lacked a Parliamentary head it suffered; adding one improved its prospects. Antipattern: leaving departments exposed to parliamentary 'wasps' without an engaged parliamentary champion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ineffectiveness of permanent clerks as Parliamentary advocates
rubrics_metrics.description: Permanent officials or clerks acting as departmental defenders in Parliament are usually ineffective: they are outsiders, subject to hostile examination, and unsuited to the combative assembly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guizot's experience: an external clerk will speak 'under suspicion', be cross-questioned, lose dignity, and may 'get hot and red' or be 'massacred by the innovators'. Such speakers lack votes and party backing and therefore cannot reliably defend departmental policy before a house of representatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bureaucracy tends to prefer routine over results
rubrics_metrics.description: A trained bureaucracy, formed by long specialist training, tends to value forms and routine above achieving substantive results; officials may come to treat procedures as ends rather than means.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supported by Burke's phrasing and the 'tailors of business' metaphor. Historical example: Prussian system becoming 'dead and formal' and failing in new circumstances (Frederic the Great and Jena). Antipattern: assuming technical training alone guarantees good outcomes in changing environments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bureaucracy tends to expand government and interfere with liberties
rubrics_metrics.description: Functionary systems centralise many social interests in bureaux, multiply inspections and licences, and thereby increase official power and interference with citizens' liberties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Laing's description: officials in Germany and France inflated into a vast civil functionary class (example: 807,030 civil functionaries in France at one point). Examples of overreach: restrictions on marriage, house-arrest for subordinates; bureaucracy often serves its own expansion rather than public benefit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of mixed leadership (non-specialist heads plus skilled officers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective administration often requires a mixture of generalist, non-specialist leaders at the top and specially trained officers below; non-specialist heads provide broader judgement and adaptiveness while specialists execute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: successful joint-stock bank boards (capitalists/board members supplying broad insight with trained officers beneath) and railway management run by capitalists rather than engineers alone. Guidance: put generalists at the top to combine specialties and see the 'end' as well as the 'means'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper role of a minister: oversight rather than execution
rubrics_metrics.description: A Cabinet minister's duty is to ensure his department is properly run, not to perform its daily work; if he does the work himself he will probably harm the department.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sir George Lewis: 'It is not the business of a Cabinet Minister to work his department. His business is to see that it is properly worked.' Ministers should act as critics and correctors, relying on permanent staff for execution; excessive intervention is counterproductive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative model must fit national character and rate of change
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a permanent bureaucracy or frequent ministerial renewal is preferable depends on the country's dynamism: a static, agricultural country may tolerate an unalterable bureau, while a progressive, changing country needs extrinsic chiefs to correct and animate administration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument: in an active, changing society, fixed bureaucracies 'cramp improvement' or are destroyed; extrinsic chiefs bring fresh minds to question obsolete forms. Antipattern: applying the same administrative model irrespective of societal pace of change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Party organisation as institutional mechanism for turnover
rubrics_metrics.description: Party organisation provides the mechanism by which heads change with ministries; turnover is built into parliamentary systems and has compensating benefits (and costs) compared with presidential/patronage systems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: American example: near-total office turnover with presidential changes and wider patronage, but the US also develops permanent elements where scale demands it (e.g., major revenue departments). Guidance: recognise party organisation as a natural provision and consider trade-offs (e.g., job opportunities for displaced officials vs. administrative disruption).
